I now come to another quotation on the same page, 1741. There the minister says this:
Therefore I come back to the point that the building of the dam never was discussed in council-
I presume that is the cabinet.
-before the 30th day of May or since.
We do make advances with the dam, for it is thirty years since it was first discussed, and in another thirty we may get something out of it. The minister is asked some questions here. The hon. member for Prince Albert was amazed when the minister said that the cabinet did not know anything about this. I am quoting the minister now, as reported at page 1744:
We have not yet discussed it with the province of Saskatchewan since the report is out, and until it is discussed we are not in position to proceed.
Or with the cabinet?

Or with the cabinet.
So it had not been discussed with the cabinet and it had not been discussed with Saskatchewan. But today we are in the assured position-we are all ready for another election-that the cabinet is unanimous and no doubt they will be doing something about the building of this dam. The Leader of the Opposition addressed a question to the minister and he obtained the same answer. This is at page 1747 of Hansard. I have one other little place marked. I did not know that I had these passages marked until I found this old Hansard report and it is tremendously useful to me today. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre got into the discussion at that point. I quote:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the minister mean the members of the government with whom he has not discussed the matter?
I think I know them as well as my hon. friend does.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But the minister says he has not discussed the question with them at all.

I have a pretty good idea what they think about most of the matters I am talking about in spite of the fact we have not discussed them.
On that occasion the minister said he thinks he knows what they think about it. I am glad that now we have got a little farther because he said today that he knows not only what they think about it but what they say about it and they are all in agreement about it. Away we go to the races for another year, and the next election.
I could go on, of course, because this subject has been discussed for so long and so much has been put on the record. I have accused the minister, I have indicted him for making contradictory statements, and probably in that case it is my responsibility to prove I am right in my assertion. I am going to give

you a quotation from one more speech that the minister made at Southey, Saskatchewan. The press report reads:
Agriculture minister Gardiner told an election meeting last night . . . etc.
I really need to read only the relative part.
This work for irrigation could be started as soon as the need for employment arose after the war.
Here we are today with more than 500,000 men out of work, and no public works shelf. We heard about a public works shelf back in 1945, but the goods have gone off the shelf now. There is not any shelf. This work for irrigation could be started as soon as the need ior employment arose after the war, says the minister.
In addition the minister told of a large program for which the plans were only partly drawn, costing $110 million in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It would involve a dam on the Saskatchewan river near Outlook, Saskatchewan.
I might have said that speech was made at a political meeting in 1945. The Leader-Post commented on that speech in an editorial as follows-I am sorry but I cannot say what the minister said. All I can do is stress these quotation marks that are here. The editorial says:
All in all, it was a valuable as well as a provocative speech which Mr. Gardiner made. What he told the three provinces and the people of the three provinces in a word was that the federal government does not need any more urging. It already has both the intention and the authority to go ahead on the four major water conservation projects named.
May I point out in that regard, too, that one of those things was the Outlook dam. There is a lot more of it. Here is something a Liberal M.P. said speaking at Kindersley. The press report states:
He stated that he had secured assurances-
I would not know where.
-that one hundred and eleven million dollars would be available for the proposed scheme.
Then, the Leader-Post of April 27, 1946, under the title "Saskatchewan dam assured", carried the following article. I shall read only the third paragraph.
The dominion government thus did not need the endorsation of the South Saskatchewan river development association to begin work on the South Saskatchewan river. It had already decided to go through with it.
I will give you another one. This one is a speech made by Mr. Gordon Ross, and perhaps we cannot hold the minister responsible for what he said. The press report states:
Tenders will be called shortly for the much discussed South Saskatchewan irrigation scheme, J. Gordon Ross, Moose Jaw, intimated at a Liberal nominating meeting here Wednesday.

As a comment I would say that would be a likely place for such a statement to be made. The date is May 23, 1946. The article continues with the following in quotation marks:
"The scheme has been worked out; much of the engineering has been done and before long some contracts will De allowed", Mr. Ross said, "and a start will be made as soon as men and equipment are available."
Well, that is that. As for the expenditure, I noticed that in his speech today the minister emphasized that this was not largely an expenditure by the dominion government, but after all the provincial government was going to pay for a lot of it. The federal government would only have to build the dam and then look after maintenance. There was not a word of that before 1951. In all those old election speeches that I recall there was not a word about it. The minister never said anything about Saskatchewan participation when he spoke in the Technical school in Saskatoon back in 1944 at the time of the provincial election. He said, "We will build this dam", and he mentioned the sum of $110 million. I see the minister is ready to get up and tell me that some of that was for Alberta.
I will not bother you.
Thank you.

You are doing yourself
enough harm; I do not need to bother.

When I made a speech in 1952 similar to this before the election the minister told me to keep right on going because I was hanging myself. The minister said that in the city of Saskatoon he had a lot of friends and I would be doing myself a lot of harm. Well, sir, I took that risk and the Minister of Agriculture was one of the five cabinet ministers who came to my city before the election. May I point out to him that I am back here now and returning his kindly visit.
With a bigger majority than ever.

Never mind the majority, but it is a larger one and one that shows a one to one correspondence in thousands to the numbers of cabinet ministers who visited our city.
It was only in 1951 that we were astonished to find, after we came back after the election, that Saskatchewan would have to help finance this scheme. The figure the minister mentioned then was the sum of $33 million for the province and that has been increasing since. It was boosted to $45 million, and at the moment I do not know where it is, but
Supply-Agriculture
the Saskatchewan government is going to have plenty of responsibility in regard to the building of that particular project.
Now, our people are getting a bit angry about this. I do not know whether the failure of this government to do anything about the project had anything to do with the results of the last dominion and provincial elections in Saskatchewan. I believe the minister would at least admit that in those elections his party was none too successful. I believe I shall leave it at that. After a while you get tired of being promised these things. You get tired of these deviations and these twistings. Even the Star-Phoenix, which is a good newspaper and usually leans quite heavily on the Liberal side, does not like these things.
Here is a clipping from the Star-Phoenix of April 29, 1953. It is headed "New Deal on the Dam", and reads:
Mr. Gardiner's suggestion for a new deal on the South Saskatchewan river dam cannot be taken seriously.
Have we got to the point where the senior Liberal member and cabinet minister for Saskatchewan cannot be taken seriously? If so, I think it is too bad. I should like to be able to take seriously the words of any cabinet minister. This article goes on:
He has been making speeches about the dam throughout the country ever since 1946.
I could correct that, for it was a lot earlier than that. I am not going to go into this matter any more, but the article concludes by saying:
Mr. Gardiner cannot escape announcing a federal
policy-
That is all they know about it, they underestimate the minister.
-for the South Saskatchewan river by raising additional questions. The reception which the people of Saskatchewan gave to the report of the royal commission should have been enough to tip him off that the people of this province are in earnest about getting some irrigation developments started long enough before the next drought to do some good. Moreover, the Saskatchewan River Development Association is not leading a delegation to Ottawa this week to be confronted with a new set of conundrums-
That is not my word.
-designed to get Mr. Gardiner or the federal government off the hook. We want to know what the federal government proposes to do about the Outlook dam.
And I want to know; and I think everybody else does, and particularly everybody else who lives in that particular section of the country.
Well, sir, I did not intend to say nearly as much as I have said; but maybe it is a good

Supply-Agriculture
thing that someone should draw attention to these statements. The minister goes out to the west and makes statements. Then he comes back and, in his usual manner, he explains them away in the house-"I meant this" or "I did not mean this" or "the reporter put a comma in"- the last time it was a comma. Do you remember the famous comma? Today it is quotation marks he objects to. And let me say if I were accused of making that statement, I would object to the quotation marks too.
I think we should have some forthright statement. I give the minister credit for wanting to have the dam. I believe he does want it. But let us know what the state of affairs really is. The Prime Minister says one thing at a meeting in Regina and the Minister of Agriculture says something else at Saskatoon. Then he comes here and says something which I, at least, interpret as being different.
Either we should drop this thing as a political dodge or we should build it. Preferably, I am in favour of building it. Meantime, if you cannot build it, then be honest about it and say so. The minister will say, of course, "I was honest and said so". He has already quoted passages to that effect. Well, what are we to take from these quotations? The minister goes out and makes these statements. They are given to us in quotation marks. If it is true that this cabinet has now decided to ignore the commission's report on the dam, then that is a cabinet decision. What is that cabinet decision? Is the cabinet decision that the dam is to be proceeded with? If it is to be proceeded with, is it to be proceeded with forthwith? Let us know.
Let me finish this speech by saying, as I said to my friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare: There are no tricks in plain and simple faith.

Mr. Chairman, although I am an enthusiastic supporter of irrigation and a supporter of the Saskatchewan irrigation scheme-when it is finally determined just what is the best scheme, and who is going to pay for it-I do not propose to follow the previous speaker in respect of his general theme.
I would like to join with those who have already spoken in expressing our rejoicing that the minister is back, and that he is rapidly recovering his old fighting form which, I am sure, all hon. members have greatly enjoyed, even though at times they may not have rejoiced over the things he was saying or what he was doing. But we do want to have him back and in a condition to say those things.

There is another reason I am glad the minister is not going to be eased out of the house by the hospital route, and that is this, that of all the men in the cabinet who have spoken in respect of the question, the Minister of Agriculture has manifested the greatest degree of forward looking in the matter of the disposal of our surpluses-getting them out of the country. The minister will correct me if I paraphrase inaccurately what I believe he said on one of his trips. As I recall it he said, in effect, that if we cannot devise means whereby we can get our surpluses into the hands of those who need them, then that fact must indicate that we are deficient or lacking in ideas.
The minister indicated clearly to me, and I believe to those to whom he was speaking, that in his opinion it was possible for us to get our surpluses into the hands of those who need them, regardless of whether or not they had anything to pay in return. And I would gather there was an implication in the minister's remarks that an obligation was imposed upon us to exert ourselves in an effort to solve that problem.
It was almost like a spring in the desert to find those words coming from the Minister of Agriculture, a minister in a Liberal cabinet at Ottawa. I am glad to see him back. I would encourage him to go straight along that line, and he will find me right behind him when he does.
I enjoyed the minister's review of the position up to the present time, although he did not tell us a great deal. He did give a few facts. I am not sure however that they were related generally to our whole problem. They did not give us any definite idea as to what we could expect in the future in relation to the stability of agricultural conditions in our country

and that is something we are all looking for, including the minister. I think it is fitting that we should lay down for ourselves some general principles in agriculture upon which we can go forward.
No one in the house needs to be told that the backbone of this nation is agriculture. If we allow our farmers to be impaired in their efficiency and in their effort to produce the needs of life, we shall seriously weaken the whole economic fabric of Canada, right from the foundation. We shall destroy the confidence which in these days of great anxiety is of much importance. To illustrate, all we have to do is to remember what happened to farmers a few years ago in the matter of hog production. They were preparing themselves to produce hogs to fill further orders, and suddenly the bottom fell right out of the market, and all the producers

of hogs in the west were, as they have expressed it, burned. Most farmers sternly resolved, in most emphatic language, that they would never touch hogs again.
We do not want that kind of condition to develop again in the west in connection with any agricultural product, because by the time the farmers recover their confidence it may be too late. As everyone knows we are in dangerous times.
Now, the principles in which Social Creditors believe are, I believe, the same as those in which all other people believe, so far as farming is concerned. The first of these is that the price of farm products to farmers must not be permitted to fall, except in accordance with a general corresponding fall in the prices of all items entering into their costs of production. For hundreds of years economies and governments have succeeded in making farmers take the rap when an endeavour was made to bring prices down in a country. I hope that we are too enlightened in this age to attempt to do that any more.
I have said on the floor of this house that prices of certain commodities had to come down. I did not mean they should come down while the cost of production stayed up. That is the first general principle. We should like to know whether the minister agrees with that and whether his department is to be guided by that principle and whether there is to be one hundred per cent backing of him and his department in the cabinet at Ottawa in the advocacy of that principle. If there is, we shall support it, the minister, his department and the government in respect of agricultural prices, and so will the people.
The second great principle is this-I am not sure everyone will agree with this, but the minister will come somewhere near agreeing with it I believe. We should have capacity production of all non-perishable foods, capacity both in respect of variety and of quantity. This is no time to begin to cut our production in reference to any of the needs of life. I believe every hon. member agrees in that respect. Well, if every hon. member agrees in that respect, let us put pressure on our government to see that they live up to it-and we can do it. The Liberal members can do it and they will have the opposition behind them in that wholesome endeavour.
The third principle is that all of the nonperishable foods ought to be stored on the farms in storage facilities accepted by government inspectors. There is altogether too much danger in this world today to have our great storehouses of food built in places like
Supply-A griculture
Fort William where a lucky bomb could blow the whole of a season's supplies right out of existence.
It is a great place in which to live.

Yes, it is a great place to see everything blown to the sky. I noticed that as I was coming by, just the other morning. They have even made those great elevators white so the enemy can locate with greater ease. I ask any hon. member whether he thinks it is safe to have this nation storing food all in such conspicuous and readily accessible concentrations as that. No one will say it is any longer safe.
There is another important matter, and that is as regards the elevators in which we store grain all over the piairies-it is easy to detect and destroy them. As a matter of fact, as the hon. member for Peace river says, they are landmarks. Imagine what a merry time a flotilla of bombers that happened to get over our guard coming in from the north would have just utterly demolishing every one of those concentrations of elevators at every important point clear down Alberta's length and breadth, from the Peace river to the United States border. Similarly with the Saskatchewan elevators; with just one blow they could knock down seven, eight, nine or ten elevators all in a row. Think of what likewise could be done in Manitoba. It is easy enough for us to be supercilious about this matter and smile, but there will be no smiles if the thing happens. There would be nothing but dismay. Let us remember that that thing could happen to you and me within the next year. What are we going to do about this? Are we to be just sitting ducks inviting the enemy to come, or are we going to do something about it? All of this indicates, in my judgment, that we should adopt forthwith a policy of storage on the farm.
The fourth principle which I think is very important is this. Let us expand our production in purposeful teamwork with the British commonwealth and the United States. I do not know what has happened to the British people and the United States people within the last ten or twelve years. We seem to have got the idea that there is no security, there is no validity in anything British or Anglo-Saxon any more. It has got to be international, or it has no virtue. Let me warn hon. members that in my opinion we shall live to see, and we shall not have to live very long, the United Nations crumble as we saw the league of nations crumble.

It has nothing in the world to do with what we are discussing at the present time, and anybody who brings it up is just plain cheap. He is not thinking about the big problems in the country at all. I had been dealing with four principles that I had laid down as being desirable in respect of our agriculture. I was urging that we keep our eyes on the British commonwealth and the United States. If others then wish to fall in line, very well, but if they do not, our foundations are not going to crumble because they fall out of line. We can be great and powerful and accomplish the mission that the Lord intended us to accomplish without having any serious complications with peoples other than our own and I do not intend any offence to anybody else.
In my judgment the fifth principle is this: Let us aim to produce for our own adequately, and then some for our neighbours. Let us be conscious of that all the time. If it is flax, if it is sugar, if it is wheat, if it is any one of all the essentials of life, let us produce adequately for our own, make ourselves as nearly self-supporting as possible, and then produce some for our needy neighbours. They are going to need all we can give them.

I have in my hand a letter dated April 23, 1954 that I have just received from the North American regional office of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations. There are passages in it which I believe we should contemplate once more and see if we cannot do something about the situation. Speaking of the food supply, here are some of the words:
However, global estimates tend to give a favourable impression, obscuring the fact that because of great differences in production between regions and countries, people in many areas have still less to eat than before the war, especially in the Far East.
Speaking of the 1953 report which has just come out, the letter has this to say:
This report gives two outstanding features of the current world food situation. One, the vital necessity of raising productivity, per man and per hectare, in the underdeveloped areas. The other, nothing less than the sheer magnitude of the world food problem as a whole, still not properly appreciated in many countries. Whatever standards are taken, some 70 per cent of the world's people are living below the present average world diet. To raise their diet to that average, itself far below the best fed countries' level, would take an additional food supply equal to the total 1952-53 production of North America and Oceania combined.
In the light of that I ask any member in the house: Can you conceive of its being a sensible thing for us to limit our production of grains and non-perishable foods like beans, corn, flax and so on? The letter continues with this quotation from the report:
"Compared with the real human needs of the deficit countries, as distinct from what they can afford to buy, food stocks now accumulating shrink into insignificance. Whatever supplies are shipped to those countries, whether in the normal way of commerce or as gifts or loans, can do no more than alleviate their real needs. A basic improvement", the report says, "in their food supply, must come primarily from a steady increase in their own production. To help forward this improvement is the main task of FAO."
I offer this comment on the letter. I have had the impression ever since we began forming these FAO's and all the rest of them that there has been an unreality about their performance. FAO, for example, is designed to supply surpluses from one country to another, but somehow or other it never enters into the minds of those in the organization concerned with planning and operating that the money has to come from somewhere. Money is the thing that counts in these matters. The result is that FAO has been just about as valuable as a fifth wheel as far as actually getting anything done in the world is concerned.
They tell me that the world still has fourteen hundred million people going to bed hungry every night. While FAO is all right as an ornament, it might just as well be written off unless we supplement it in a way

that will really make it able to do its job. I believe the men in charge want to do the job.
There is another quotation further on in the letter which I think it is important for us to have. It reads as follows:
. . . and the task of finding some solution to the problem of distribution is one of primary importance.
Of course it is, but I ask hon. members how many times they have heard anyone in this house suggest a means of increasing distribution. Outside of the Social Credit group, who has suggested any means that could increase distribution? I ask them to read the newspapers, the big wise, know-it-all newspapers like the Ottawa Journal, the Toronto Globe and Mail, the Windsor Star, the Montreal Star and all the others that can tell us all about how to run everything.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do not forget the Winnipeg Free Press.

Oh yes. When have they ever said one single word about how to improve distribution? When have they ever done anything except to attack and assail those who did try to offer suggestions? That is a serious matter. I did not name all the offending newspapers, but the pathetic thing is that throughout the nation from coast to coast and throughout the United States this matter of distribution is the one great problem we all recognize but never try to do anything about. Somebody has got to do something about it. And may I suggest that we cannot do something about it if we use only the old measures which have been tried and tried and proved wanting ad nauseam.
Here is another short quotation. The letter writer has been telling about how FAO had referred this particular problem of distribution to a working party-noble little working party; Canada is a member of it! A bright lot of information it will get from Canada, especially if Canada sends the Minister of Finance because he has never offered a suggestion in his long life about how to increase distribution. He will not even listen to suggestions of any kind. I say that right to his face, and I do not blame him for not answering, because I know he cannot answer that point. Neither he nor any other member of the Liberal party has ever made any effective suggestion to this house as to how to deal with the problem of distribution. All they talk about is free trade, but free trade has been tried for thousands of years and has never succeeded yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Higher and higher protection.

That is just as foolish.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Everybody is stupid but our John.

Everybody likes to get
away from the heat, but you don't have to go to the point of freezing. What you want to do is to find the proper place in between- the middle road.
Now this is what it says about this working party which has been working away something like the group of brilliant Canadian men who went to the Bretton Woods conference and signed an agreement. They sat around and listened to a lot of communist spies telling them stories and selling them a bill of goods. They then came back and pretended they had achieved something wonderful. But all they had was a gold brick. But here is what this writer says about this working party:
The	working	party was	in	no position tofind a	complete	solution to	this	question of surpluses,	but they	did review	and	draw up recommendations for	several types of	special arrangements for surplus disposal, at least in line with existing supplies and to prevent the accumulation of new surpluses.
Now, is that not a bombastic way of saying they did nothing? It is a most effective way of telling people that the working party could do nothing and never will do anything as long as such parties are composed of people who cannot look into the future as the Minister of Agriculture was evidently endeavouring to do when he suggested that if we could not find a means of getting surplus goods into the hands of those who need them there must be in us a deficiency of ideas. Let us get the ideas. They are around and they can be found. Back in 1915 our fathers had the ideas as to how this thing of distributing could be done, and they did it under the finance acts of 1914 and 1923, as I indicated on April 28 in my talk.
And so, there are five things that need to be said about this question of agriculture. First, let us see to it that we do not force our primary producers to take the rap in our endeavours to bring down the cost of living in this country. Everyone knows that the cost of living should be brought down. As I have already indicated, however, we should not force the farmers to bring it down and crush them under the burden, without bringing about a corresponding reduction in their costs which now are becoming so onerous. To suggest that the farmers should carry this burden is an improvident and most fallacious proposal. Secondly, we should work for the greatest possible degree of production of every kind of which this country is capable, and we should concentrate on the production of goods which will not perish such as beans, peas, corn, all the grains,

sugar, and the like. Third, we must store these commodities on the farm and provide adequate storage facilities. Fourth, in all our efforts we must work in co-operation with the British commonwealth and the United States. And fifth, we must produce as far as we possibly can all the things we need ourselves and some which are needed by our neighbours, and then see to it that those neighbours get those goods.
The question might be raised as to how we are going to finance all this. Well, I have already said enough about that. In my speech on November 17 I went into that question in detail and I also dealt with it in my remarks on April 28, and I challenge any man in or outside of this house to find any flaw in the suggestions I made. I do not care who he is.
To say that we cannot take from the Bank of Canada money to provide the storage facilities is simply to talk nonsense. If we cannot take that money out of the Bank of Canada then we had better replace the Bank of Canada with the Finance Act of 1923, because under that act they were able to do it. To say that we cannot take the money out of the Bank of Canada to pay the farmers for their grain after it is put into storage is once more to be unrealistic. To say that we cannot take money out of the Bank of Canada to pay the farmer for the storage of the grain while he takes care of it on his farm is once more to be unrealistic. And to pretend that taking money out of the Bank of Canada would cost the taxpayer anything is thoroughly unrealistic. This would apply to all that is required in storing all the different kinds of non-perishable goods which Canada can produce over the next ten or fifteen years. Let anyone who thinks he can answer those statements get up right now and try.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these are the Social Credit proposals in regard to the problems facing our agricultural industry. If we adopt these proposals, and back the Minister of Agriculture in his endeavours to make the agricultural industry of Canada greater and greater in the years ahead, I will guarantee that with his leadership it shall be done.

Mr. Chairman, the minister in his speech this afternoon contended that the farmers in Canada are now in a better position than at any other time in their history. That is a contention with which I think he will find the farmers of this country cannot agree, and certainly the statistics do not bear it out. In spite of that, however, the minister devoted almost all of his speech to an attempt to prove that that statement was true, except for that part which he

devoted to the South Saskatchewan dam. I am not going to deal with that matter.
However, with the aid of a few statistics available to me in the house at the moment, I would like to demonstrate that the group of figures which the minister put on record covering the cash income of the farmers during the period from 1943 to the present time, and which he used with the evident idea of trying to persuade the house and, of course, farmers throughout Canada that they are better off now than ever before, do not prove that at all. As a matter of fact, there are other figures which show that the reverse is the case. The minister dealt with the cash income of farmers over three-year periods and, as I have already pointed out, he did that evidently for his own purpose because if he had put them on the record on a year to year basis it would have given us a much better indication of the amount of income, cash or otherwise, the farmer earned during the past 11 years.
The minister stated that the farmers' cash income for the last two years amounted to $5,574 million. The estimate, including the third year-which would be the year 1954, he must mean-would bring this up to $8,200 million. That means that he has estimated the cash income for farmers for this year, 1954, as $2,626 million. On what basis he has estimated that figure, goodness only knows. Certainly the budget figures that were produced will not bear out any estimate of that kind. In other words, he has estimated about the same cash income as the average for the two years preceding, namely 1952 and 1953; and 1952 was the top year which we have ever had as far as the farmer's income is concerned. Nevertheless, the minister is estimating just about as much as the average of those two years. What they were separately, I do not know. I do not think for a minute that that estimate can be taken very seriously.
When the minister was attempting to do this same thing last year he did not use the figures of cash income. I have here a copy of Hansard of April 27, 1953, and this is what he said then as reported at page 4440. He dealt then with the net income of farmers:
Net income to farmers from the sale of farm products reached a peak of $2-2 billion in 1951. Estimates for the net income received in 1952 are placed at just under $2 billion. There is some indication that this present satisfactory position may be maintained.
In view of that statement, it is interesting to look at the figures produced by the Minister of Finance as to what the net income of farmers was during these past few years. As a matter of fact, the minister was not even accurate in the figures he gave to the house

last year; that is, if the Minister of Finance is accurate in the budget papers he has produced, and I am giving the Minister of Finance credit for being accurate in those budget papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you.
Maybe they were both wrong.

In this year's budget papers at page 3760 we find set out in table 1 the national income and gross national product. There we find the net income of farm operators from farm production in 1950, and that figure is given as $1,503 million; in 1951 it was $2,106 million. That is the year in which the minister said it was $2,200 million. In 1952 it was $1,934 million and then in 1953 it was $1,667 million. It is getting on toward $300 million less in 1953 than it was in 1952.
I do not think there is anybody here who will maintain that prices are not still falling, that they have not fallen so far this year, that they are not less than they were in a similar period last year, namely, 1953, or that there is not the prospect of their falling, particularly those of grain, from the levels that were secured last year. The chances of the prices being less are great; in fact, prices are almost certain to be less. In view of that consideration, I find it difficult to understand the minister's trying to sell the idea that the farmers are better off than they have ever been before. As far as cash income is concerned, they are less well off or they were less well off in 1953 by the difference between $1,667 million and $2,106 million or in other words approximately $400 million less well off.
In view of these figures which show what the net income position of the farmers is, it is quite certain that the estimate that the minister made of what their cash income is going to be, namely $2,600 million, just is not correct and cannot be correct as far as this coming year is concerned.
In addition to that, of course we have to relate the income that farmers have received to the prices that they have to pay for the goods they buy. They have not heard that there has been any great reduction in the price of farm machinery, fertilizer, binder twine, insecticides or any of the other materials which farmers have to purchase in order to carry on their business. In other words, the cost of carrying on farming operations is just about the same as it has been or has declined very little, whereas farm income has declined considerably.
The statistics which my colleague the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand was using a while ago from the bureau of statistics with regard to the index numbers of farm prices

Supply-Agriculture
for agricultural products of course show clearly in another way what is shown by this table about the net cash income. Looking at the figures from year to year, we find it is rather noteworthy that the high point was reached back in 1951 when the index for the price of farm products was 296-8 and that it has now declined, as of January of this year, to 233-2. That is a very serious decline. During the same period, as I say, the prices of the things farmers have to buy have not declined.
A little comparison with regard to farm prices and the cost of the things farmers have to buy is given in the Searle Grain Company's weekly report of October 7, 1953. It states:
The current index number, compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics, of the costs of the things prairie farmers have to buy for their living and production now stands at 226-4 compared with 100 in 1935-39. This means that it takes $2.26 in the hands of prairie farmers to have the same purchasing power today that $1.00 had before the last war. This, therefore, means that the total payment on wheat so far to be made of $1.72 a bushel has a purchasing power equal to 76 cents in 1935-39. This is for No. 1 Nor. Fort William, but this $1.72 equals only $1.54 to farmers at the average country point, which $1.54 has a purchasing power equal to only 70 cents in 1935-39. The initial payment of $1.40 for 1 Nor., but which at the average country point equals $1.22, has a purchasing power equal to only 54 cents in 1935-39.
In other words when you relate to the actual amount the purchasing power of the money received by western farmers for their grain-for their wheat, particularly-you see that the price that they are receiving for the wheat is a low price. It is not a high price at all. That, of course, has served greatly to confuse the issue so far as farmers are concerned and so far as the people of the rest of this country are concerned. When they see farmers getting $1.78 a bushel for their wheat-if that is the price of wheat- they say that that is a high price. But as I pointed out today, actually what the farmer on the farm is getting is about 70 cents a bushel in terms of the purchasing power of 1935-40 money, and it is therefore looked upon as a low price for wheat.
The Minister of Agriculture went on to deal with certain specific products in an effort to bolster up his contention that farmers are better off now than they were before, and he had something to say about cattle. If we look at the price range of cattle during the past two years we find that, by and large, cattle prices are about half what they were two or three years ago, that is taking all grades of cattle into consideration because the price drop in some of the poorer grades has been greater than that of the quality steers. However, just paying attention

to the price of good quality steers, 1,050 pounds, on the Toronto market in 1951, we find they reached a price of $34 per hundred. They remained at $34 a hundred or right around that figure for the most of 1951 and particularly the latter half of it. Then the price dropped and has continued to drop until in today's Globe and Mail I noticed they are quoted at $18 to $19 per hundred. The price has been almost cut in half. This is a very serious drop, especially when you take into consideration the lower grades of cattle. We find the price is very little more than half of what it was in 1951.
In spite of this the minister says the farmers are better off under those circumstances. How could a cattleman be better off? He is certainly worse off. In fact, a considerable number of cattlemen have experienced a lot of trouble, particularly those who bought cattle at the high prices that prevailed in 1951, and have had to sell those cattle at these lower prices.
The minister dealt with the question of hogs. He professed himself as quite satisfied with the cattle picture, and said we had better markets at home and in the United States than we could get anywhere else in the world, so everything was all right. The fact that we may have better markets at home or receive bigger prices at the moment for what we are producing now than we would receive anywhere else in the world, is perhaps a matter for some satisfaction. Nevertheless it is not much satisfaction to the man who is only getting half as much as he did two or three years ago. Certainly, that man is not nearly so well off.
When we come to the question of hogs, we find the price is quite high now and has been for the most of the past year. The reason for the high price of hogs is to be found in the machinations of this government. The policy of this government that led to maintaining grain prices at unduly high levels is partly responsible, as is the announcement that the floor price would be cut off. This encouraged the farmer to get rid of hogs as fast as he could. As a result there was a cleaning out of hogs about a year and a half ago at a time when they were selling for around $20 or $21 a hundred. They are now up to $34 or $35 a hundred.
At that time many people got rid of sows which were due to farrow, so an artificial scarcity of hogs was created. This artificial scarcity is a direct result of the policies pursued by this government. The minister expressed great pleasure over the fact we were not producing more pork than we could consume in Canada. The inference is that we do not need the large overseas market for

bacon and pork products that we enjoyed for many years. We can eat everything we produce. The only reason we can eat everything we produce in the way of pork is that the policies followed by this government have created a scarcity. We could produce a great deal more pork than we are producing.
If we were doing so we would not have the difficulty we are having now with the large surplus of grain. The destruction of the hog industry in this country, as a result of the policies pursued by this government, is responsible for quite a bit of the surplus grain we have. If we had maintained our overseas markets for these pork products, particularly for bacon in Great Britain, we would be producing a great deal more pork and the hogs would have eaten up a great deal of this grain. In other words, the policies this government has followed have aggravated and aggravated these various farm situations.
Now the minister had something to say about the butter situation. He believed there was nothing to worry about, but I would think there is likely to be quite a bit to worry about. I notice that the National Dairy Council of Canada is getting quite worried. Every week or two they send me a lot of literature in connection with the matter, pointing out the very large surplus of butter we have on hand at this time as compared with other years. This particular circular is dated April 30, 1954, and it shows the stocks of butter on hand as of that date. There were 45-6 million pounds on hand, and the circular lists the stocks of butter on hand as at that date during the years from 1932 to 1954. The stocks this year are the highest we ever had. In 1950 there were 28-4 million pounds and last year there were 27 million pounds. The other years are down to 5, 11, 6, 12, 9, 11, 6, and so on. That was all the surplus butter there was at that date. We are holding this large amount of butter at a time when we are just entering the butter producing season.
The minister believes there will be no difficulty about it, but I do not know. He said the government might suffer a small loss. So far as I can see the only way they are going to get clear of this surplus is to sell it at practically give-away prices. If that is done the people of this country will probably have to add a considerable amount of money to the government fund.
The minister devoted a certain amount of time to the wheat situation. He stated that the marketing this past year has been close to usual. I do not know just what that means, but certainly if the figures on the disappearance of grain mean anything-and I think that
Supply-Agriculture
is the only thing we can look at-then the disappearance for this past year has been quite small in comparison with other years. I have not the figures here, but I looked at them yesterday and the disappearance for this past six months has been considerably below normal. If the minister is talking about the whole year 1953, that is a different matter.
So far as the past six months are concerned there has been a considerable slowing up in the sales of grain. The minister went on to say that the large amount of wheat we had on hand was due to the large crop we had during the past three years. He said that we now have a year's crop on hand. As a matter of fact we have on hand considerably more than a year's crop. The biggest crop we ever had was two years ago when we had 664 million bushels. We now have on hand, according to the best estimates I can secure, about 741 million bushels. The minister said that if the sales of wheat continue about the way they have in normal years and we have a normal disappearance, everything will be all right.
Well, everything will not be all right. As a matter of fact, if we did not grow one bushel of grain next year, and just the normal disappearance took place, we would still have a very large amount of wheat on hand-far too big a carryover. If we grow only a small crop next year, then by this fall again we will have an enormous carryover. As a matter of fact, if we grow another good crop-and if one may judge from the present weather conditions there is every prospect of another good crop this year-we are going to be in an almost hopeless situation so far as storage facilities for grain are concerned. We will be in a position where there will not be room in the elevators for anything like the amount of last year's crop, and there will be no room whatsoever for this year's crop. Therefore I presume there would be no opportunity to deliver any of the new crop.
So the wheat situation in Canada, particularly from the point of view of making delivery of the wheat stored or on hand, is extremely serious. I do not think the minister is doing the farmers in this country any service when he attempts to minimize that situation. Instead of that, the minister and other members of the cabinet should be making plans right now for the handling of next year's crop, so far as storage is concerned.
Many farmers will not be in a position to buy lumber to build granaries, and there should be some payments to the farmers who have grown the crops so they can carry on their farming operations. These are extraordinarily pressing problems, and the government should be taking steps right now to

Supply-Agriculture
meet them, instead of sitting with folded hands hoping that the best will happen, or probably that there will be a crop failure, or something of that kind. Because, unless the government is hoping for a crop failure, there can be no logic whatever in just sitting and doing nothing.
There is no use closing our eyes or attempting to deceive ourselves by blinking at the truth, because the general situation is considerably poorer than it has been for a number of years. It is just the exact opposite of the picture the minister tried to give us today. For several years he was in a very happy position, because every year prices were going up. That happened for some time after the war, although there was a setback in 1950. But, apart from that, prices went up year after year; and year after year he came into the house and said that things were better this year than last year, that there was more money in the farmers' pockets, and so on. There had been some recession last year from the high of 1951; but this year it is certainly ridiculous to say that the condition is better, or to attempt to fool the House of Commons and the farmers of this country.
Instead of that the minister should face the situation, because it is a serious one. On behalf of the government he should state what they are prepared to do to solve some of these problems.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the statement made this afternoon by the minister regarding the South Saskatchewan dam. However, I must confess to some disappointment in what he said. He left the impression with us that while he and the government had not done anything toward building the dam, since they had not done anything against it we should therefore be satisfied. I am afraid that proposition will not find general acceptance among the many people of Canada who are looking forward to the commencement of work on that project.
Like the hon. member for Saskatoon, I am particularly interested in the South Saskatchewan development because I represent a city which over the last few years has grown by many thousands in population. It is a city that is vitally dependent upon the agricultural prosperity of the surrounding country. I realize that there is nothing that will contribute as greatly to the economic wellbeing of Saskatchewan as the building of the South Saskatchewan dam. The minister has pointed out on many occasions what this dam would mean not only to the farmers directly concerned but also to the hamlets, villages and cities of Saskatchewan.

I would like to feel that this is a matter of national importance. I suggest we should rid our minds of any thought that this is a project that will affect only a small part of the country because, after all, agriculture is the basic industry in Canada. I believe that in Saskatchewan we have almost forty per cent of the cultivated acreage of Canada. Certainly we do possess a great part of Canada's farming land. The welfare of any one part of Canada is reflected in the welfare of the country as a whole.
The Prime Minister has intimated the national importance of this particular project. On June 28, 1952, speaking about some of the projects then being considered in Canada, one of which is nearing completion -I am referring to the Canso causeway-and also referring to the St. Lawrence seaway project, he said, as reported at page 3945 of Hansard for that year:
The third project was the South Saskatchewan river project. This is of particular interest to the central prairies, but it is also of interest to the whole of Canada to have Canada developed in such a manner that there will be no depressed areas in this country.
We know that one of the projects to which he referred is now nearing completion. We have had repeated assurances that a start is going to be made on the St. Lawrence seaway project. And I want to say I am certain that members from all parts of Canada welcome the building of that seaway. I am certain all members from my own province are pleased to see works of public importance, whether they are being constructed in the maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia or anywhere else in Canada. We have to view this situation in a national sense and recognize, as the Prime Minister pointed out, that the South Saskatchewan river dam project is something that is not just primarily for the benefit of the people living in that geographical area, but something which will contribute greatly to the economic well-being of Canada.
It is not my intention to go into the detailed history of this project. In previous years the matter has been dealt with by various members when speaking in the house. But I do remind hon. members that the project will accomplish two purposes: First of all it will offer some insurance against conditions which existed in my province only a few years ago, a period of time during which a good percentage of our people were on relief. We suffered from practically every unfortunate occurrence nature could inflict upon us-[DOT] drought, soil drifting and weed infestation. We know during that time the serious condition that existed in the livestock industry. We know many animals were lost, while some

were shipped to community pastures. We know about the great quantities of hay that were moved into Saskatchewan.
All that is history. But we should remember that these conditions could very well return. As a matter of fact we know that in 1945, 1947, 1948 and 1949 hay was shipped to Saskatchewan from points in Alberta and Manitoba, in some cases at a cost of $10 a ton. We know those conditions have occurred in recent years; and we have no guarantee that nature is going to smile on us in the future so far as rainfall is concerned, or that we will be spared the disastrous drought conditions that are being experienced in certain states of the union to the south of us. There is no greater method of protecting and insuring against a national calamity in the particular area such as that than by the building of that dam.
Apart from the negative aspects of the building of the dam, a great contribution of the building of the dam would be to Canada, not just to the geographic area of which Saskatchewan is a part, but to the dominion as a whole. Without going into any unnecessary detail, Mr. Chairman, I just want to summarize as briefly as I can and suggest that this project, as the hon. member for Saskatoon has pointed out, was initially a federal project. I recall the minister making statements.
I always enjoy listening to the minister at a political gathering. If he is speaking at a meeting within a reasonable distance I usually make an effort to go to hear him, and I recall his speaking in glowing terms of what the construction of this dam would mean to Saskatchewan and to Canada as a whole. I recall that all during that time there was no suggestion at all that this was to be a joint project; it was going to be a project built by the federal government. Then, after many promises had been made during the 1945 campaign and in 1949, which the hon. member for Saskatoon quoted. In 1953 we heard similar statements. The Regina Leader-Post of June 23, 1949 is reported as quoting the minister as saying, as may be found in Hansard of February 9, 1953 at page 1769, as follows:
The South Saskatchewan project would provide power and encourage building of industries in small towns, provide an incentive for young people to stay in this province. "I think we have made a fairly good start now," said Mr. Gardiner; "send us back to complete the job."
In the last campaign we had similar assurances given on behalf of the minister. I hold in my hand a clipping which appeared

in the Regina Leader-Post of July 14 last headed: "Liberals certain to construct dam." The article continues:

speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. It is now just about a minute and a half to six o'clock. I understand that the Minister of Finance wishes to table a report which must be tabled today.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was discussing the change in the nature of the proposed South Saskatchewan dam. I had pointed out that over a period of some years the dam had been promised by the minister and his followers in our province, and that at that time there had been no intimation whatsoever that this was to be a joint project between the federal and provincial governments. Then we were confronted with a new development when the minister made it known that the federal

government would be prepared to proceed with the dam if and when the provincial government was prepared to take some part in the building of the dam.
As I pointed out, this came as a distinct shock to people generally of all political parties because up until that time there had been no suggestion that the federal government considered it anything other than a strictly federal proposition. Not only did this change take place but the minister went the full circle last year because, when speaking at Indian Head just prior to the last election, he suggested during the course of his remarks that if the province wanted the dam built it should go ahead and build it and that it was primarily their responsibility.
Far from being a federal responsibility, it was first of all said to be a joint responsibility and then the minister went so far as to say that it was primarily a provincial responsibility. If he really believes that I would draw his attention to the fact that from 1934 to 1944 there was a Liberal provincial government in Saskatchewan and from 1935 on we have had a Liberal government at Ottawa and if the minister, as he suggested last July, felt that if the province wanted the dam it should go ahead and build it then I suggest he should have made that suggestion to Mr. Patterson who was premier of the province from 1935 to 1944.

If my hon. friend will permit me, I am sure he does not want to misrepresent the matter at all. He will recall that it was not until 1946 that either the site of the dam or any other matters that made it possible to build it at Outlook were announced.
That is an interesting comment. I have not the information at hand but I think by going through the files I can find references to the dam prior to that time.

I am not saying there were not references to the dam. The dam was not promised by me but was advocated by me for many years prior to that. I did not promise the dam. I simply advocated that it ought to be located and built.
There is a fine distinction in words there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Very fine.

The minister says that he did not promise it but simply advocated it. The way the minister can advocate something makes it sound very much like a promise, and while the minister may have felt that he was advocating it I feel quite certain that his audiences were under the impression that he was promising it. This afternoon the

hon. member for Saskatoon was wondering whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Minister of Agriculture was more adept at skirting or avoiding a question or issue. The Minister of National Health and Welfare took that as a compliment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They both are.

When I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture is a past master at it perhaps he will take that as a compliment. It is a compliment in one sense when one is speaking about political sagacity and adroitness, but viewing the problem from the point of view of those who want to see the j ob done I do not think it is quite so complimentary.
Be that as it may, the minister interrupted me and said that he did not promise the dam at an earlier date but merely advocated it. I am quite certain, however, that the people were left under no illusion as to what the impression was that he sought to leave with his audiences. With respect to the project itself, may I say that I am speaking of the project as a whole. I assume that the storage of the water was and is even today considered a federal responsibility. Now when the people in the province of Saskatchewan found that the federal government was now going to require the provincial government to pay part of the cost they might well have felt that the Liberals had been kicking this football around for a great number of years, had been advocating the dam, if not promising it-I will use the word "advocate" -and that it was now up to them to put up. They might well have felt that the Liberals had been attempting to win elections on this promise long enough and that it was about time to deliver the goods.
But I am proud of the way in which the people of Saskatchewan viewed the matter. They did not view it from a political standpoint at all. The natural tendency would have been for the people to say that they had been tricked and fooled over the years by the federal authorities and that the federal government was now trying to welsh on their promise to the people. Instead the provincial government took, I think, a very co-operative attitude. They had been under the impression that it was a federal responsibility, but instead of harpings and recriminations, instead of denouncing the federal government the provincial authorities were extremely co-operative. When it was announced that the provincial government would be required to pay a part of the cost they stepped in right away and made an offer to the federal authorities on the basis of what they considered to be their fair share of the costs.

I have here copies of the correspondence which passed between the premier of the province and the Minister of Agriculture. I am not going to refer to it directly because I believe many of these letters were placed on Hansard last year by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. However, I think the correspondence indicates quite clearly that the provincial government stepped in immediately and said:	All right, we are disappointed that the federal government is not going to treat this as a federal responsibility but the main thing is we want the dam built and we are prepared to bear a share of the cost.
I think the minister will agree that in each successive stage of the protracted and apparently fruitless negotiations that have been carried on over the past several years between the provincial government and the federal government the provincial government has shown its good faith and willingness to co-operate in every detail. I think there can be no doubt on that score. Various objections have been raised from time to time, and I should like to refer to an editorial in the Star-Phoenix of July 9 last, under the heading "Blockage Upstream". It reads in part as follows:
. . . Mr. Gardiner outlined three requirements that would have to be met before the federal government could make a final decision on the project. The requirements were: 1. Interprovincial agreement on the use of the water required for the project.
2.	An offer from the Saskatchewan government which would remove any suspicion that the federal government was subsidizing the cost of the power development connected with the undertaking.
3.	A realistic estimate of the cost of the project, to settle the conflict between P.F.R.A. figures and those contained in the Hogg report.
With respect to the first point, an interprovincial agreement on the use of water was required for the project. It was very interesting last summer just prior to the voting to see the tremendous amount of space devoted in the press in the west to this whole question of getting the right to use water from the Alberta government. At that time, just prior to the election, Liberal speakers were able to go out and say that we could go ahead with the dam but the Alberta government was standing in the way. It was a very fine whipping boy to use just prior to the last federal election though, of course, we know that this has subsequently been cleared up by the announcement that there was no longer any obstacle in that connection. Therefore, point No. 1 has been removed as an obstacle to proceeding with this project.
Now, the second point was the offer from the Saskatchewan government which would

remove any suspicion that the federal government was subsidizing the cost of the power development connected with the project. Here again, the premier of the province in a number of letters to the Minister of Agriculture, and later publicly, announced the provincial government's willingness to pay for the hydro generating plant and pay for part of the cost of the project in order to remove any possibility that anyone in Canada might feel that this project was in any way subsidizing the power users in the province of Saskatchewan. In other words, I think any doubt that might be in hon. members' minds regarding any suspicion of fear that there might be a subsidization of power development has long since been removed.

Mr. Chairman, just on that point I think if hon. members follow the report which has been read to this house from that particular group they will find that in Saskatchewan last week I stated that the two matters had been settled to the satisfaction of this government, and the point with regard to the part of the cost which the provincial government will pay if the project is proceeded with is still under discussion.

I quite agree with that statement, Mr. Chairman, because I know that in the initial correspondence between the premier of the province and the minister the premier did set out the exact figures. The minister wrote back and suggested that what the federal authorities required was not a set of exact figures but some general agreement to share part of the costs. In other words, the province went so far as to be committed to a definite set of figures which the minister apparently felt was not necessary at that time. While that may be at present under negotiation I think that at no stage, at least up to the present, has there been any reluctance or any unwillingness on the part of the provincial authorities to meet the Department of Agriculture and come to some agreement in regard to sharing the cost. In other words, at no stage has there been any reluctance or unwillingness on the pari of the provincial government to share part of the cost in the construction of this dam.
With respect to the third point, a realistic estimate of the cost of the project to settle the conflict between the P.F.R.A. figures and those contained in the Hogg report, I am certain that when the decision to appoint a royal commission to investigate this matter was first announced it caused a great deal of consternation among people, particularly those who had not been following the development of this project. I believe the minister himself is on record as having said some very uncomplimentary things about this report.

I am not sure whether his comment was "silly dam report" or "dam silly report", but at any rate I have clippings here, though I do not wish to take up the time of the house in reading them, in regard to various Liberal members who also expressed themselves as being very sceptical or unconvinced as to the need for this commission in the first place.
I am not too sure as to the number of years, but I believe the P.F.R.A. has been interested and has investigated this project for nearly 16 years, and I think we can have confidence in our P.F.R.A. engineers. I do not think any hon. member has suggested that the government is lacking in qualified personnel. These people have been working over a good many years, very often in the field and covering the entire province, and they have a full understanding of irrigation problems within the prairie provinces. They have had considerable experience along these lines as the result of many, many years of research and they have arrived at an estimate of what the dam would cost.
I understand that the original estimate was $101 million, but in view of the intervening years one would have to add the increase in costs which has taken place and I believe this cost certainly would not exceed 30 per cent over that period of time. That would bring the cost of the dam up to about $135 or $140 million, but in any event the P.F.R.A. engineers on the ground who have done a tremendous amount of work in this connection presented the government with a set of figures. The government chose to disregard these figures and set up a royal commission which asked a private corporation, the Mannix corporation, to investigate and submit other estimates. We know that the report of the royal commission was not too kindly received by those who were interested in the project irrespective of their political beliefs, and I am sure the minister himself was not too pleased with the findings of the commission.
At that time the provincial government, presented a brief in reply to the royal commission in which it took each item of the report point by point and it makes what I think are critical observations of the royal commission report. I certainly do not intend to deal with this at this stage, but I do feeL the points raised by the royal commission have been quite effectively met, although I am suggesting that there might be some disagreement.
I think all those who are interested in the construction of this project will agree it is a fairly accurate estimate of the findings of that commission so that when I read in a newspaper a few days ago that the minister

had stated in Saskatchewan that the government was prepared to forget the report of the royal commission, and I heard the minister's explanation this afternoon in which he said he did not say these things or rather he put his own interpretation upon what he is reported to have said, then I was not at all surprised. The minister is always running into difficulties by saying something and afterwards having to explain what he did say and very often his explanation is at variance with what the average person who heard him in the first place would suggest he said.
Therefore, irrespective of the minister's footwork this afternoon in explaining what he meant in his statements in Saskatchewan, I suggest that the people out there hope that he meant precisely what he said, namely that the government has forgotten about the royal commission report. If that is the case, Mr. Chairman, then indeed the last of the obstacles has been removed. In other words the question of the water rights has been settled as it affects the province of Alberta, as has also the question of the provincial government offering to bear part of the cost. I have not heard any evidence to the contrary and judging from the correspondence between the provincial authorities and the Department of Agriculture that does not seem to be any great stumbling block. If the province is quite prepared to bear a share of that cost, and if the minister says that the government is prepared to forget the report of the royal commission then I suggest that the last obstacle towards the commencement of the project has been removed.
If that is the case then I feel that we should proceed immediately with the construction of that dam because the minister is on record as indicating how valuable a contribution that dam would make to the economy of the prairie provinces and of Canada generally. I think the Prime Minister is also on record. I have noted a couple of quotations in Hansard with respect to the debate last spring in which he seems to be quite satisfied that it is not a purely local matter at all but is a project to the general advantage of all Canada.

In order just to clear the air in connection with the matter we are now discussing, I think that I should say this. When I was here this afternoon I was not as fully informed as I am tonight. I met the provincial government last Saturday and discussed the only matter which is still waiting to be determined before it is again presented to the government here. We discussed there the proportion of the cost the provincial government should take on if the dam is proceeded with. I had a letter this afternoon

I am not saying that the provincial government is responsible for it at all. It is just a matter for negotiation. It takes some time to determine the matter when you are going to spend $60 million or $100 million.

I realize that the minister has information that we do not possess. I mean that, after all, there are negotiations which are being carried on. What I suggested during the course of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, was that up until the present time-that is up to the point that we have knowledge of- the province made its offer right in the letter from the premier of the province. For example, on February 10, 1951, when the premier wrote to the Minister of Agriculture, he pointed out in part:
Our understanding is that the federal government is prepared to accept full responsibility for the construction of a dam. the estimated cost of which is to be in the neighbourhood of $68 million. It was further suggested that the distribution system at an estimated cost of $19 million and the cost of levelling the land for irrigation, which is estimated at $6 million, were to be the responsibility of the provincial government and the water users who will benefit by this project. It was also suggested that the installations for the generation of hydroelectric power at an estimated cost of $8 million were to be the exclusive responsibility of the provincial government. While this is not the allocation of costs which was suggested when this project was first proposed, if this is the only basis on which the federal government is prepared to proceed with the project, I do not see that we have any alternative than to base our discussions on the allocation which you outlined to us.
My colleagues and I are most anxious that the South Saskatchewan river development project shall be proceeded with at the earliest possible date. As soon as the federal government has announced its intention to proceed with this undertaking we are prepared to negotiate and sign an agreement on the basis of the allocation of costs outlined above.
In this letter the premier commits himself on behalf of the province of Saskatchewan to a definite undertaking in so far as the sharing of the cost is concerned. Here is my point, Mr. Chairman. At that time the federal government did not say, "Oh, we cannot go ahead with it because we are not satisfied with the proposition; we do not feel you are going to pay enough." That was not suggested at that time. Now the minister says that is one of the things that is holding it up. During the time of this correspondence and over these past several years the obstacles and impediments to proceeding with this project did not deal with the question of the allocation of costs-up until the present time at least. Other reasons have been thrown out but as far as I can see from
