the correspondence, the question of the allocation of costs has not been the important point.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has said that this should not be a political matter or should not be a political issue but that it is a business proposition and should be handled as such. All I am suggesting doing is this. If he reads my letter of April 24, 1953 to the government of the province of Saskatchewan he will find that there are four propositions made there. One is that the water rights would be cleared up. In Saskatoon last week I stated that the water rights are cleared up to the satisfaction of this government. Another proposition was that the provincial government was to give us an undertaking that when the water was once put into the dam, they would use it for some particular purposes. They have agreed to use it for the purposes which were outlined by the P.F.R.A. organization. That was the second point. The third one was that some provision had to be made which would warrant us in believing we knew what the cost was going to be. In Saskatchewan last week I stated that those three points had all been taken care of and that the one that is still left is this one we are now talking about, namely the part of the cost of the dam itself which will be paid by the province and the part which will be undertaken by the federal government if the project is undertaken.
Your halo still does not fit.

I am glad to hear that statement from the minister. I do not know whether we can take it from that statement that when this matter of the allocation of costs is settled we are going to see the commencement of the construction of the dam. I want to suggest that this matter has been dealt with before. We have had correspondence and we have had assurances on the part of the minister that when these matters were settled they would go ahead. But each time we just sort of got on a dead-end street and found that we were confronted with something else. I certainly hope that the minister's statement here indicates that when this matter has been cleared up as between the federal government and the provincial government, there will be a commencement.
I would draw to the attention of the minister the fact that when the premier of the province telegraphed the Prime Minister last spring with regard to this matter, he asked the Prime Minister for assurance on two points. I think I have the exact wording of the telegram. It reads in part as follows:

I am in receipt of letter from Mr. Gardiner asking provincial government to submit proposal for construction South Saskatchewan dam. Before submitting proposal or discussing agreement essential that we have from you categorical assurance on two points, first that you are now convinced that South Saskatchewan river project represents best use that can be made of water available, and secondly that federal government prepared to proceed with this undertaking if government of Saskatchewan assumes fair share of costs.
That was last spring. These negotiations have been going on for some time. When the provincial government made an offer initially and suggested an exact sum of money at that time as to what their share would be, the minister replied that that is not what they wanted; he indicated that they did not want a definite figure at all but that they just wanted something to kick around, something they could discuss.
I am quite certain that the minister is perhaps quite sincere in his assurances that perhaps something can be done, but I do not know just whether the minister's assurances are enough.

Just to clear up the point
entirely, Mr. Chairman, may I say that there is not anyone who has yet said that the dam was going to be built. That fact should be absolutely understood. No one has said the dam is going to be built. However, the question of costs and all that are being considered as between this government and the provincial government. All I can say is that if agreement is reached as between the two governments with regard to all the points, there is a possibility that it will be proceeded with. But up to the present time on every occasion that the federal government have discussed the matter with the province they have said, "We are discussing it under the absolute understanding that no undertaking has yet been given that the dam will be built".

I do not know just what the minister means when he says that no undertaking was made by the government. If there was no undertaking by the government, may I say this. The people of Saskatchewan were certainly led to believe that there had been an undertaking by the government.
The hon. member just does not understand-
I do not want to make a political speech. If I did, I would be prepared to read-
Oh, oh.

-quite a number of quotations from the speeches of prominent Liberals campaigning in the 1945 election campaign, the 1949 campaign and the last campaign. In

the Rosthern by-election the people were told that if they sent Makaroff to Ottawa, that would be tantamount to repudiation of this great scheme. How can you repudiate an undertaking that was never given? The minister now says no one ever promised to build the dam. When he was campaigning during the by-election in the constituency of Rosthern it was said that if anyone but a Liberal was elected it was a repudiation of this scheme. I might say that not only during the Rosthern by-election but throughout many campaigns this has been a stock political football for the Liberal party. They have certainly made use of it in the last three federal elections. Just how effective it has been, I do not know, but certainly they have tried to use it as an effective political weapon. nothing about it until it was announced. I believe the Liberals thought they would get those votes, but I doubt that they did.

I want to congratulate the minister upon his return to health. When he returned to Ottawa from overseas, I thought he had had it. He did not look very well. He had a faraway look in his eyes. When I saw the minister in such good form this afternoon, I could not help but think he had improved wonderfully. I hope it continues; I am serious when I say that. However, one thought did occur to me when he was speaking. I cannot tell the committee the difference in the number of farmers in the east as compared with the number in the west, but I venture to say that not more than a third of them are in the west.
More than that.
Well, there might be half, although I do not think there are half of them in the west.
Not half.

In his figures this afternoon, regardless of the fact that not even half of the farmers are in the west, the amount given for the east was $2,128 million as compared with $2,258 million for the west. In the next three-year term the figure for the east was $2,871 million and for the west $3,348 million. The next figure given for the east was $3,605 million and for the west $3,952 million. The next figures the minister gave were $3,444 million for the east and $3,129 million for the west.
The last figures were only for two years.

The fact remains that the figure for the west was still high. And that brings me to this point, where I say that those of us in the east are not receiving as much consideration as are the farmers in the west. Certainly we are not making as much money, and we work a lot harder to get it.
That brings up another point. That is the real reason why there is more income tax paid in Saskatchewan, per farm, than there is in Ontario. One does not need to look for another reason.

I grant you that, because of this fact. The cash return in the west is available; the tax collector can get the figures quite readily. And it is a pretty difficult matter to sidetrack the income tax branch. In the east the farmers do not have much in the way of income, because they do not make enough money to pay income tax. Very few farmers in the east are in the income tax brackets. The department has put forth an extra effort in the last year or two to collect more income tax from the eastern farmers and, while it may have been having some success, it is not having as much success as was expected when the drive was put on. However, I am not ready to discuss that subject in detail because I do not have the figures with me at the moment. I will discuss it before the estimates are completed, or perhaps I may have a chance in the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Finance when the subject of income tax paid by farmers is before the committee. I say the farmers are not being dealt with fairly in that regard.
This afternoon the minister made reference to a three-year average. The farmers are given a chance to take a five-year average and if, in some cases, they have not made a return, they are put on a net worth basis and they are not permitted to consider the lean years with the good years. I think that is a mistake that should be corrected.
In the last few years the government has been very anxious to sell farm produce so long as there was a good market for it. But when the marketing situation got tough, then the responsibility was thrown back on the farmers themselves. That was what happened in connection with cheese. Anyone can sell on a buoyant market. There is no trouble in getting rid of products when everybody wants to buy them. It is when there is a surplus that there is difficulty in selling. The cheese people took the bit in their own teeth. The government cannot take credit for it. The cheese producers were able to dispose of their cheese, and we find a 83276-272i
Supply-Agriculture
position where the cheese industry is in a rather healthy state. This is due to the effort they put forth themselves.
And due to the fact that the cheese situation is somewhat better, the butter manufacturers have been placed in a better position, too. But it will be found before the next six months is up that the minister will have a lot more butter on his hands than he has now. When he cannot get his supply down to around 20 million pounds at this period of the year he certainly will not get it down farther between now and the period of flush production of milk.
I am going to say something now about the hog situation. A year or so ago when, under the minister's policy, the price of hogs was lowered to the extent of 3 cents, how long did it stay there?
It is 23 cents today.
Did it ever get down to 23 cents?
It went down close to that in the month of January; but it went right back up.

Yes, it went right back up. As a matter of fact, it went up to 28 cents inside of a month, and it has been going up ever since. But during that period of time- and this is the joker-when they were afraid they were not going to get paid for their hogs a good many hogs were marketed, including brood sows and every other kind of hogs, both little and big, many of which were not fit to go on the market. They were all shot out on the market, with the result that we were short of breeding stock. Then, of course it does not matter how high the price goes, if no one has anything to sell. The only reason now we are consuming all the pork we have is because we do not have the pork. But a year from now the minister will be saddled with a position in which he will find supplies of surplus pork to worry about.
This afternoon the minister said something about cattle. Let me give a concrete example of how much money we made out of cattle in the last few years. I shall describe my own experience, because I know exactly what I made-and I am no different from many other producers. As a matter of fact, I am in a much better position than many others were.
Anyone who bought heavy cattle or two-year-old cattle in 1951 took a decided loss. We all lost 10 per cent, right off the bat, at the time of the foot-and-mouth disease. Perhaps that was not the government's fault, or the fault of anybody else, but we took a 10

Supply-Agriculture
per cent drop right there, and the situation never righted itself. Stocker cattle were selling for as much as 36 cents a pound in 1951.
I happened to buy forty head at that time.
I felt there was going to be a drop in the price of cattle, and I bought small ones. Anyone who bought small cattle managed to get his money out of them, but those who bought the heavier cattle in 1952 not only lost their feed but they lost a considerable amount of money in addition to that. They had to sell them and they lost large amounts of money.
In my case I did not have to sell in 1952, because my cattle were not the proper size.
I could not get in 1952 what I paid for them, after feeding them for a year. The result was that I kept them another year. At the end of the second year-that is, last year-I sold them. At the end of the second year I got 18J cents a pound on cattle for which I paid 36 cents. I did not lose any money in dollars. As a matter of fact, I had $1,200 after feeding for those two years, but it did not pay for the chop they consumed. I am not the only farmer. I got off pretty lucky.
A lot of farmers who bought heavy cattle, or two-year-old cattle, in 1951, not only lost their feed but they lost pretty nearly half of what they paid for the cattle. They have not redeemed themselves yet. A lot of these fellows are still working away. I do not feel so sorry for those who were in the cattle business for several years and had a chance to make a little money, but I do feel sorry for the younger men who just started up and had to pay a lot of money for those cattle. Mind you, the bank will only carry you so long as your risk is good and then you have to sell. Because they could not cover their notes they had to sell their cattle, and those are the fellows I feel sorry for. A lot of them were in that position.
That is the position in which the cattle business is today. Since last fall cattle have been holding pretty steadily; in fact, much better than I expected they would. Those of us who bought cattle last fall found that tops were going at about 18 J cents. They are still worth 18i cents. I heard of a sale made the other day at 21 cents. Those cattle went to the United States. They were an exceptionally choice bunch of cattle and consisted of two or three loads. If cattle stay around 20 cents or 18 cents I have no doubt that some of those boys will make a little money this year, but that is all in the future. We are hopeful that that will happen.
As I said before, the government was ready to accept the responsibility for selling produce of the farm when selling was good, but now that it is difficult to sell they are throwing

it back to the producer and letting him do the best he can. I do not believe in subsidies. In the first place, I believe we would have been better off if we had never had any. We would have learned to take care of ourselves and not depend on the government. Too much dependence is put on the government and the individual is losing his initiative. This country was built on personal initiative, and until we get back to that there is no hope that the government will pull us out of all the difficulties that we face.
I do not think I have any more to say at this time. As the items go through I shall have more to say. I must say one thing. On going through the estimates of almost every minister's department it will be found that nowhere is the government making any attempt to lower administration costs. No other business in Canada, including agriculture, could operate like that. In every other business a decided attempt is being made to cut costs. The reason why producers' costs are so high, both in manufacturing and in agriculture, is that taxes are too high, and those taxes have to be paid first. Until the government makes some attempt to lower departmental costs we will not be any better off.

I should like to make a few references to the speech we heard this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture and also to mention a number of points which are of particular interest to the farmers of Manitoba. In his speech this afternoon the Minister of Agriculture informed us that in his opinion the farmers have never been in a better position than they are today. I am not going to dispute that at any great length, but I should like to quote a different point of view of a person whose opinions will carry some weight. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Globe and Mail dated March 8 of this year, which quotes a former premier of Ontario speaking at a conference. He was speaking to the annual meeting of the shareholders of the First Co-operative Packers Limited of Ontario. These are his words:
As things have been going we cannot, I think, avoid a crash. The symptoms are now disturbingly close to those that preceded the crash of 1929.
He was discussing agriculture generally, and those were the opinions he expressed at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Who was he?

Mr. Drury, a former premier of Ontario. Somewhere between the statement we heard this afternoon and the rather gloomy forecast made by Mr. Drury is the situation which exists in agriculture. Figures already produced in this debate have shown

that there has been a rather serious decline in the income of farmers generally. A little later on I shall put some more figures on the record in that connection.
I also wish to refer to another statement, and I was rather surprised to hear the Minister of Agriculture say this. He said that in his opinion a floor price is not necessary under cattle or beef, or whatever the term was he used. That does not seem to meet with the opinions that I have heard expressed by farmers in Manitoba, at least. I am not in a position to speak for farmers in Saskatchewan or elsewhere; I confine my remarks to the farmers with whom I am familiar.
I hold in my hand a copy of a brief presented to the Minister of Agriculture in February of this year by the interprovincial farm union council. This farm union council represents the three farm unions of the prairie provinces; that is, of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I have no doubt the minister will agree that the members of this council are men and women with a great deal of experience in agriculture, some of whom have had previous experience in government in various responsible positions, and I think their opinions are worthy of consideration at this time. What do they have to say about the livestock situation? I should like to quote from their brief where they refer to livestock prices. These are their words:
The livestock industry's present position is serious and should have the immediate attention of the government. Livestock producers have taken a severe beating during the past two years, and from all available information it appears that the situation may become even worse. From figures available we find that in 1906 there were 1,181 cattle per thousand population in Canada and in 1952 there were only 635 cattle per thousand population; this shows that there is no oversupply of cattle today. Furthermore, we note that stocks of meat in storage on December 1, 1953 are 13 million pounds less than one year previous, which shows that we are not producing much of a surplus.
May I just stop for a moment to point out that with the latter part of that statement the Minister of Agriculture apparently agrees, because he said this afternoon that there is not a great surplus of beef products in Canada at the present time. The brief goes on:
Yet prices during the past two years have declined approximately 50 per cent.
I have no doubt that these figures are based on statistics which are authentic, and if that is so then certainly it is a far cry from the impression that was left this afternoon. A drop of 50 per cent in the price of livestock products certainly would indicate that the producers of livestock at least are not in the best position that they have been in for years.
Supply-Agriculture
Fifty per cent on cattle.

All right; we will accept that. Let it be cattle, but it does not say so in this brief. I continue:
In view of this, can such a drastic price decrease be justified? We believe it is time that a full investigation of the livestock industry in Canada be made-right from the situation of the primary producers to that of the ultimate consumers.
That was in February, and in the same brief the farm union council suggested that they were interested in a livestock marketing board. From time to time there have been discussions about a livestock marketing board in the house as well as in the provincial legislatures. The attitude taken by the Minister of Agriculture-he will have to say if this is still his attitude-has been that this is something for the provincial governments to look after. Apparently the farm union council is quite willing to go along with that idea, but they have placed a proviso in their brief, and I think a very wise one. They point out that the federal government has taken the attitude that the provinces should take the initiative in setting up livestock marketing boards. They are agreeable to going along with that, but here is the proviso:
Provided suitable floor prices are assured to the actual producers by the federal government, the farm unions have indicated their willingness to go along with you on such a proposal and would draw to your attention that we have taken the lead in calling two livestock marketing conferences on the prairies-the first in October of last year, and the second in January of this year-where the actual producers were invited, and did attend. At these conferences it was decided to begin drafting an improved plan for livestock marketing, using provincial legislation where available and in those provinces where the majority of livestock producers are ready to proceed, looking forward to the establishment of an interprovincial producer-controlled marketing agency in the near future, utilizing existing federal legislation to provide the needed co-ordination in livestock marketing.
Since then there have been one or two additional conferences, and if newspaper reports are correct the minister was present at one of them at least. In Manitoba twc conferences have recently been held, one under the sponsorship of the Manitoba farmers' union, which was largely attended, and the meeting of approximately a thousand farmers almost unanimously agreed that there should be a livestock marketing board under existing Manitoba legislation. I understand that the same situation exists in the province of Saskatchewan so far as the organization there is concerned. Apparently there is some difficulty in Alberta because I understand there is no provincial legislation at the present time providing for the establishment of such a board. However, that situation may change.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I apologize for having to interrupt the hon. member but I am doing so on his behalf. I would ask committee members that if they have to carry on conversations to do so as quietly as possible. I do not think it is fair to any hon. member who is trying to address the house or to those who are trying to listen to him.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. As I was saying, perhaps the Minister of Agriculture was not even aware at that time of the statements being made. However, surely the minister must have been made aware of the facts after having received a visit from a small delegation while he was in Saskatchewan. That delegation on returning from their visit to the minister, and here I only repeat what has been said by others, left the impression again that if the province of Manitoba would make a request to the federal government assistance would be forthcoming.
From that time on many of us made great efforts to have a request forwarded from the province of Manitoba to the federal government for this special assistance believing in good faith that since statements had been made, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture had said that he would be willing to consider such a request, it would
Supply-Agriculture
be for the benefit of the farmer to do so. But as the correspondence piled up we found there seemed to be the same tendency as is displayed in this South Saskatchewan dam situation that certain statements are made and then people start backing away from them. Here I would like to quote from a letter from the premier of Manitoba to the Minister of Agriculture dated December 12, 1953 discussing this whole situation of special assistance which I had requested in the house.
I was not alone in making that request for the same request was made by municipal officials and provincial members. However,
I would like to read this paragraph from that letter:
I might mention in regard to this whole question that to my knowledge there has been no suggestion from the federal government that assistance, other than that given under the P.F.A. Act, would be forthcoming if the province of Manitoba so requested.
Now I will have to accept his word for that.

There is another letter
besides that one.

Yes, there are a couple of dozen letters but I am not going to take the trouble of referring to them all. This is an important phase of this matter because up until the time I received a copy of this letter, which the premier of Manitoba was good enough to forward to me at the same time as it was dispatched, I was fully under the impression, and so were hundreds of farmers and municipal officials in that area, that the federal government was willing to consider a request from the province of Manitoba for such assistance.
It now appears that the premier of Manitoba had no such assurance. The result of this was that instead of obtaining special assistance the province of Manitoba had to attempt to obtain an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in order that the farmers in that area, and of course in similar areas elsewhere, would receive benefit under that act.
To give some justification for that requested amendment to the act I should like to place some figures on record. I have here a set of figures which set out the contributions made by farmers to the prairie farm assistance fund under the one per cent levy, and also the payments made out of that fund. I will give them only in round figures. Farmers in the province of Manitoba from 1939 to 1952 made total contributions of $11,903,857.84 and to that we must add the 1953 payments amounting to $516,719, because the latter figure is not included in that first total. The two figures together

Supply-Agriculture
bring the total contributions to a little over the $12 million mark. When we turn to the benefits received during the same period we find that from 1939 to 1952 the benefits received in Manitoba amounted to $3,394,546 to which we must add the 1953 figures totalling $500,128 which brings us to a total of nearly $4 million which is about one-third of the total contributed. In other words, for every three dollars contributed by the grain farmers of Manitoba since 1939 under the one per cent compulsory levy they received only one dollar from that fund in return.
Due to that we find that later on towards the end of the session in the Manitoba provincial legislature a resolution was introduced by Mr. Stinson, who is the leader of the C.C.F. group in that parliament, in these words:
That In the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of requesting the federal government to grant emergency assistance to farmers who suffered crop losses due to flood damage in northwestern Manitoba in 1953.
That, of course, was in line with all the other representations that were made. However, the government of Manitoba apparently did not approve of that resolution in that form so a government member moved an amendment so that the amended resolution read as follows:
That this house urges the federal government to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in order that Manitoba farmers who suffered serious crop losses due to excessive moisture conditions in 1953 receive further assistance.
Those last few words are rather important. May I repeat them: so that they may "receive further assistance". This resolution or amendment apparently was not framed for the purpose of amending the Prairie Farm Assistance Act only for future years but also so that if the amendments were made, farmers in Manitoba could receive further assistance with regard to 1953.
A copy of this amendment no doubt was forwarded to the government here. I also raised the matter several times in the house asking the minister whether the amendments would be recommended. Finally we were told not so long ago that the government had no intention whatever of bringing in these amendments. At this time I should like to plead with the minister not to close the door.
The situation in Manitoba, as I have already pointed out, is such that the farmers have contributed to the fund three times as much as they have received out of it. That situation is owing to the way in which the act operates. In Manitoba there is interest in starting a crop insurance scheme which, incidentally, was suggested by the minister himself in one of his letters to the minister

of agriculture in Manitoba. However, as we know from experience, the setting up of a crop insurance scheme at the provincial level at this time is a thing that is not going to come about quickly. We know that investigations were made in Saskatchewan and Manitoba as far back as 1939, 1940, 1942 and so on-and perhaps even before that-into the feasibility of setting up a crop insurance scheme on a provincial basis and that nothing has come out of it.
Even though that committee has been set up by the Manitoba legislature to look into the matter again, I am sure that it will be years before that province will be in a position to take action on a crop insurance scheme; and even then they might have to ask the backing of the federal government in order to underwrite the scheme so as to make it successful. In the meantime I think a good case is made out, not only for the province of Manitoba-and here I am not just making a plea for the constituency of Dauphin or the other two that I have mentioned, namely those of Churchill and Portage-Neepawa which are more urgently involved at this time-but for similar areas in the other two prairie provinces. I think there should be set up some system of zoning under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in order that farmers in those areas at least have the hope or the possibility of benefiting equally under the act. As the situation is now, the scales are unevenly balanced to the detriment of Manitoba; that is not something done deliberately but that has been the result. In the province of Manitoba, or at least in part of it, we suffer more from flooding than from drought. As a result, when it comes to a matter of applying the act, even if it is done in the most lenient manner possible, it just is not possible to give the kind of compensation the farmers deserve.
I am going to recommend that the minister consider under the act a zoning plan under which, after studying crop reports over a period of years-and all those figures are available-it should be possible to set up zones with different yields as the qualifying yardstick. At the present time the yield is set at eight bushels per acre on the average on wheat. There are some areas in which wheat is not a suitable yardstick. There are some areas in which the figure of eight bushels is certainly not a suitable yardstick for a qualifying figure. Certainly northwestern Manitoba is not, because our crop yields on the average are higher than those in most parts of Saskatchewan, and the farming is done on a smaller scale. As I pointed out, flooding and hail affect crop yields in a different manner than does drought. It is not the over-all picture. It is spotty. So I

am going to recommend that the minister consider the idea of zoning so that in certain areas we could have a qualifying figure of eight bushels as at the present time but in others perhaps the figure should be twelve bushels. In others it might even be fourteen bushels, depending on the over-all long-time average yield.
There is another justification for such zoning for qualifying purposes, and that is the actual cost of production. It is well known that in the dry areas of the province of Saskatchewan, for example, or in Alberta summer fallowing is a much simpler and less costly operation than it is in northwestern Manitoba or, for that matter, in northeastern Saskatchewan. Where there is much more rain, where conditions are different and the land is heavier, it is necessary to work the land much more thoroughly and much more often during the summer months, a procedure which of course entails much greater expense. If crop conditions are normal the farmers are, of course, compensated for that expense by having a heavier yield. But if they have a loss owing to flood or hail or some other cause, the amount of money they have put into that land is much greater than it is in the case of, say, southwestern Saskatchewan or the drier areas. I therefore believe it would be only fair and just to set up a zoning system in order that farmers may have an equal opportunity at least of benefiting from this act.
As the situation is now I may say quite frankly to the minister that there is a great deal of discontent with the act in the province of Manitoba. The premier of Manitoba has stated on behalf of this government that he is definitely dissatisfied with the act. He has stated on occasion that Manitoba should cut itself entirely away from the act, should have nothing to do with it and should set up its own crop insurance scheme, all of which is all right provided that he has a crop insurance scheme to put in its place. At the present time the province has not such a scheme. I for one do not go along with the premier of Manitoba on that matter. I think that we should not cut ourselves away from this act until the province has a crop insurance scheme to put in its place, or something which would be better. But the over-all picture in Manitoba is that unless this act can be amended so as to give the farmers of Manitoba a better break than that which they have been receiving, certainly the province of Manitoba would be justified in eventually breaking away entirely from this act.
There are one or two other things about this act that I think need some changes. For
Supply-Agriculture
example, there is the provision under which lands bought or purchased from the province after a certain date-I believe it is 1940-are not eligible for prairie farm assistance. At the time this provision was placed in the act there may have been some reason for it, but since then it has certainly worked a hardship on some of the farmers. Those farmers are not exempt from the one per cent levy. They still have to contribute to the fund one per cent of the value of their crops just like anybody else, and they feel that they are being discriminated against if they are denied the benefits of this act to which they are obliged to contribute. I think consideration should be given to making a change in that respect.
In closing I want to say just a word on this question that I have tried to discuss as calmly as possible, although I feel strongly about it. I think that on future occasions we should not have a repetition of what happened where persons make statements like those which were made in the town of Dauphin about the end of June, making it quite clear that the federal government was going to come to the assistance of these farmers and these statements are accepted in good faith, and then later on the people are told that there was no such intention. I think that sort of thing is not good for public relations. I do not think it is good for the Liberal party. I do not think it is good for government. I do not think it is good in any respect. I think that statements like that are the kind of statements which bring into contempt the statements of politicians across Canada. I think we have a duty to the people of this country to keep them informed accurately and honestly at all times. Even though I cannot see how those statements could have brought any political advantage-no doubt they were designed to bring political advantage or were an attempt to bring political advantage but I fail to see how they could have done so-those statements were made. Then they had to be eaten by those persons who made them.
As a result, there has been a great deal of bitterness and bickering in the province of Manitoba since last July. Of course now we know where we stand. The federal government has told us quite plainly they are not going to do anything in this respect. The premier of Manitoba has made it quite plain he intends to make no such request of the federal government. I am not, therefore, laying any blame at the doorstep of the Minister of Agriculture. Certainly the people who made those requests and those representations were justified in making them on the

Supply-Agriculture
basis of the statements that were made to them by the Liberal politicians at that meeting to which I have referred.

In view of the fact these estimates will probably not come up again for several days there are one or two things I should say in reference to some of the questions which have been raised. I do not want to enter into a discussion about the last question which was raised, except to say this. After the first meetings which were held there was considerable done. I am not saying that everything was done that those meetings requested, but everything was done which could possibly be done under the present terms of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and that amounted to considerable. It was not simply a matter of forgetting all about it, and not doing everything that could be done under the act as it is now drawn.
The other matter about which I wanted to say a word is the floor price on cattle, and beef particularly. The member for Dauphin has gone into that in some detail, and I only want to say that I agree with what he has said, that I did attend one of the meetings held in western Canada recently, the one which was held in Saskatoon last week. This question was discussed at that meeting. I do not believe Alberta was represented at the meeting but the Manitoba farmers union was represented as was the Saskatchewan farmers union. Representations were made at that time, and they were the same as the submissions to the government that were read to us here.
We discussed this question for the greater part of the afternoon, and they reached the unanimous decision which was contained in the press statement later. It was somewhat of a withdrawal from the position taken in the resolution that was read by the member for Dauphin. What I want to say concerning the matter of a floor price under cattle or under beef is exactly what I said to the gathering in Saskatoon. I said I did not think there was anything to be gained at this time in putting a floor price under cattle as our surplus is sold in the United States, the highest market there is in the world. If we were to establish a price higher than that as a floor price, then there would be enough beef from the United States come over here to entirely ruin our markets and put us in a position of not being able to sell. On the other hand, if we were to set a price lower than the price being obtained now, then the natural thing would be to suggest that we were indicating the price was too high.
With those two matters placed before them the committee asked what alternative we had to suggest. I stated to them that we had the

co-operative marketing act of 1939. Under that co-operative marketing act we could set up a marketing organization to make it possible to do the same things as we have done for cheese in Ontario for two years, and which we are asked to do again this year; the same as we have done for potatoes in the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. In other words, we could guarantee an initial payment not to exceed 80 per cent of the average price for the last three years. I stated to them that there was only one case in which we did make the average 80 per cent. In most cases it was 60 per cent, and in some cases it was less than 50 per cent. In any case we guaranteed the organization so that they could go to the bank, raise money and whenever they took delivery of whatever the product may be they would be in a position to make an initial payment to the farmer. Then, the organization proceeds to sell the product and when they realize a price for it, they divide the money amongst those who form a part of the organization.
I repeat what I suggested a moment ago. After they had discussed that, and discussed it very fully, all of those present at that meeting stated they would make these representations the next day to the general meeting. I understand they did make them on Friday of last week, and that the idea was supported at that meeting. Under that legislation you do not have what is generally called a floor price. There is no attempt made to guarantee a price to the producers, but there is an effort made to set up a pooling organization of which all the producers can be a part. They have their own organization to sell their product. My intention in saying what I did was to impress upon them that we thought it was better to proceed under that legislation, which is already on the statute books and which has worked successfully in 96 out of 98 operations since 1939.
When I say it has operated successfully, I am speaking as a member of the government. When we set up the act we hoped to be able to make such arrangements with the organization that was benefiting by it that there would not be any payment necessary on the part of the government. Now, we miscalculated on furs and we did have a considerable amount of money to pay on furs at the end of the war. This was largely because prices were high towards the end of the war, and when they dropped rather suddenly the government had to pay some of the guarantees it had made.
The second case in which we will probably have to make some payment this year is the guarantee for the potato growers in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

The guarantees made were higher than the prices received for the potatoes when they were sold. The producer gets his initial payment, and if there is a loss occasioned the federal government pays it. On the other hand, if there is a profit made there is a distribution of those profits to the individuals who were part of the organization set-up and who delivered products to that organization.
As I say, we discussed it very fully, and after having discussed it fully there was this attempt that is being made in Saskatchewan. I assume it will have its effect in Manitoba as well. The attempt being made in Saskatchewan is to organize first a livestock board to handle the livestock under the provincial act. Then they suggest that they may come to this government in order to get a guarantee which makes it possible for them to make an initial payment so the farmers can carry on until their product is sold. Then they will again come here if there are any profits in order to get permission to pay out, having indicated that there will be no loss to the government here, and they will make further payments to the farmers.
The legislation is there, and I just wanted to say tonight, while the question was being discussed, that those are the reasons why it was not thought wise to put a floor price under cattle at this time. There is, as you know, a floor price under hogs of 23 cents which has been referred to by the hon. member for Huron. The only time the price has gone down close to that was a period which the hon. member for Huron mentioned, when the farmers were putting their hogs on the market in much greater numbers than the market would readily take them. That was during the month of January, when they thought that the lowering of the guaranteed price or the floor price was going to result in the lowering of the price of hogs. They thought that, and they delivered hogs in great numbers and almost succeeded in forcing the price down to 23 cents. But immediately that process had been carried through, the price went back up. And the prices have been the highest since that time that they have ever been in our history.
It is true, as the hon. member for Huron said, that those who stayed in benefited by that, and those who got out did not benefit. But I would like to call to the attention of western members the fact that the production of hogs has gone up. In the province of Saskatchewan as of the month of June in the year before last I believe they had over 400,000 head of hogs on their farms. Last year in June they had almost 50 per cent more, with a figure of something more than 600,000. In the province of Ontario-and I 83276-273J
Supply-Agriculture
think the hon. member for Huron will agree with this-they have succeeded through the years in holding the numbers of hogs in Ontario up to a point higher than they were even during the war. And while we in Saskatchewan had 1,700,000 hogs during the war and dropped down to almost 400,000, the province of Ontario went up after the war, and it continued to go up until this year. I do not think they have quite as many this year as they had a year ago. But that reduction in Ontario started to take place under the high prices, not because the prices were lower.
Hogs have been selling across Canada during this past year at anywhere from $42 or $43 per hog up to $50 or $55. Everyone in the house who has raised hogs will know that that is not a price at which one loses money, even at present costs. The returns are fairly high. There is a floor price of $23 under hogs. The price has been up in the $30 bracket during the greater part of the time since that floor price was put on.
In connection with cattle, the situation is as I have outlined it. I doubt very much if it would be to the benefit of farmers-as a matter of fact I am convinced it would not be-for us to put any floor price on that we could put on at the present time. The regulator of cattle prices is the prices in the United States. As the hon. member for Huron said, there have been cattle going to the United States during this last week at $21 per hundredweight.
That was paid here for them.

Yes, that was paid here for them, and it means that all the costs-duty, freight and so on-were paid. They were landed in the United States at some point where they were slaughtered at that rate. There is great sympathy for the farmers- particularly the young farmers-who came into the cattle business in 1951, as was described by the hon. member for Huron. Those who came in in 1951 and bought cattle at the prices then prevailing certainly took a loss. But the older men who have been in the cattle business for a long time were in a different position. I have talked to a good number of them in the last week or two and they have told me they made good money prior to 1951 on a rising price. They have handled about the same number every year and many of them were in a position to take the loss which they had to take as a result of having bought at the peak price in 1951 and selling at the lower price in 1952 or 1953.
But I understand well the position of the young men. Indeed, I was in that position at the end of the first war, myself. I lost most of what I had, and certainly all I expected to

Supply-Agriculture
gain by going in. The price did go down. It went down a long time as it did following the last war. I agree that the young people who have gone in now have had some difficult experiences. However I think the hon. member for Huron will agree that those who bought their cattle last fall and fed them during this winter have done very well.
It would take quite a while, even at the gain they could make this year, to make up the loss they had to take following 1951. But we hope it will not be necessary for them to do that and that they will be able to go along in this line of business. Operating on the American price they have a floor which is as high and as strong as any floor could be-whether this government were to put it on, or whether it was put on in any other way. The American market is the natural market for our surplus. Our cattle go there; and if the market here will not stay close to that price, then they will go there in greater numbers.
Our marketings in the United States in the last year have not been very high, the reason being that apparently we were not prepared to accept the prices which were paid. With hogs as high in price as they were people were more inclined on this side of the line to eat more beef. And a great number of the cattle which have gone into the market have been consumed here in the form of beef. But we are still convinced that the best floor price we can have at the moment, and probably for some time to come, is the American market, with the American price. That is the reason why we have not thought it was particularly wise to put on a floor price for cattle this year.
I think that is all I need to say tonight. There are other matters I should like to refer to at a later time. I did think, however, that these matters should be discussed now rather than to leave them over until next week.

Mr. Chairman, most of the remarks I wish to make on agriculture can be made in the discussion on particular items. However I wish to take this opportunity to deal very briefly with one particular subject which is somewhat dear to my heart, and which I am sure is very close to the hearts of a great many of my constituents, and that is the unfortunate lack of co-operation between various departments in the federal and provincial governments. On several occasions this has seriously affected agricultural development in my constituency.
In passing I might say that the constituency of Kootenay West produces only about 16 per cent of its total food requirements. Therefore it can be seen that there is a great opportunity for expansion of agriculture in

that constituency, particularly when it is known that we have thousands of fertile uncleared and unsettled acres. What are the principal reasons for this? The principal reasons are lack of transportation and lack of public investment in irrigation, drainage, schools and hospitals, as well as in public services such as lighting and telephones.
I readily admit the good work that is being done by both the federal and provincial governments departments of agriculture; but there is a lack of co-operation that I think is very necessary for the proper settlement of this part of the country and for the protection of our farmers. This lack of co-operation between the federal departments and the provincial government causes difficulties in my constituency particularly-I am speaking from experience-for those who are farming at present and prevents many others who would wish to farm to take advantage of the many fertile acres which are only awaiting public investment on the part of governments, federal and provincial, and the application of industry and labour on the part of individuals. To illustrate that point I must mention that while we produce in my constituency only some 16 per cent of our total food requirements, we have some 16,000 acres of undeveloped fertile agricultural land in the Lardeau valley, of which the greater portion is black soil bottom land. We have thousands of undeveloped acres on the Arrow lakes and thousands of acres idle in other parts of my constituency remaining undeveloped because of the lack of co-operation that provides the public investment and the public services that are necessary if this land is to be settled by the people who want to settle it.
The federal government is responsible for P.F.R.A., and I shall have a little more to say about that under the item in question. Great work can be done under P.F.R.A. in British Columbia, and particularly in my constituency. There is the Department of Veterans Affairs interested in settling veterans. There should be the greatest co-operation between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Veterans Affairs and the provincial departments concerned. The federal department can do something to promote agriculture and to give some guidance to the development of these new areas in the establishment of not expensive but small illustration stations, that would be of help to settlers, because our conditions vary greatly within a few miles. Then there is the question of co-operation between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Public Works. Very often the lowering of a river by some dredging or the removing of some log jams or something of that sort

lowers the water table of the surrounding land and provides additional opportunities for farming. In the last three years the lowering of the Duncan river as a result of the removing of snags and obstacles has lowered the water table in the surrounding land so that 3,000 or 4,000 acres can be farmed to better advantage.
Then, we have the federal government responsible for unemployment. What an opportunity for some co-operative planning and to use many now unemployed in all these projects. The provincial government is responsible for roads, hospitals and schools and for the provision of light and power facilities and for telephones. All that is required is a common-sense approach and the development of more co-operation instead of the unplanned approach with both the federal and the provincial governments going their own ways, and federal departments and provincial departments carrying on without any co-ordination of their activities. What we need is a co-ordinated approach and a co-operative approach on the part of all agencies, federal and provincial.
I want to illustrate that by a recent happening in my constituency which could have been prevented, I believe, if there had been some co-operation between the federal departments and between the federal government and the provincial government at an earlier stage, and some activity on the part of the Department of Agriculture to protect the farmers' interests in my constituency. I refer to the plight of the farmers and the fruit growers on the Arrow lakes who are left stranded because of the discontinuation of steamer service on the Arrow lakes.
In the early days that district was settled as a result of promotion activities in London largely by the government of Canada, the government of British Columbia and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Most of the early settlers in the Arrow lakes district, as they were in the Kootenay district, where our good chairman comes from, were green Englishmen who suffered the full consequences of their greenness after they arrived. I remember one settler in the Arrow lakes, a Dr. Kelso, who made particular inquiries in London of the Canadian Pacific Railway when he bought a tract of land in the Arrow lakes district where we had a steamer service in operation, and which was an excellent service. He inquired whether it would be maintained. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company's officials said to him and to many others intending to settle on the land in that area that not only would they guarantee to maintain the present service but if anything it would be improved.
Supply-Agriculture
That is the basis upon which the settlement took place. Many of those people in those isolated communities have spent a lifetime clearing the forests and clearing the land, planting orchards, making fields and developing farms; their whole life experience, all their capital and all their labour have been devoted to the development of their small ranches during the last half century. All their investment is in that district, where suddenly, with thirty days' notice, the Canadian Pacific Railway discontinues the steamer service on the Arrow lakes, with a callous indifference to the needs of the farmers and settlers who settled in the district in the early days. The company's officials did not even have the courtesy or the decency to give those affected at least six months' or a year's notice of the discontinuance of the service so that they could arrange for some other service. At the present time the farmers in my district who want to get out to Revelstoke from south of Nakusp have to engage to travel on non-scheduled aeroplane flights and this is most expensive. At the present time there is no provision to transport the freight, express and passengers in general, from Nakusp to Arrowhead.
I bring this to the attention of the minister because in a situation like this the federal Department of Agriculture should have been interested in the plight of these ranchers, and so should the provincial government and the provincial department of agriculture. Here are people who were brought into this country by government and C.P.R. advertising, who have devoted their whole lives to the development of the country and have made a great contribution. Suddenly on thirty days' notice, they are left without transportation facilities and their whole established routine is upset and disturbed.
At the present time every effort is being made to have some service established on certain portions of the lake, and I urge that the Minister of Agriculture do everything he can to support the activities of the West Kootenay and central farmers' institute, and the various fruit growers organizations and the other organizations in the district of the Arrow lakes who are trying to find some way now to re-establish a service which will give them an opportunity to travel, to ship their hay, their fruit, their other commodities, such as cherries and produce of that sort, north to Revelstoke, or south to the Kettle Valley railroad. I emphasize again that this is an excellent illustration of an unfortunate happening to 3,000 people, the

Supply-Agriculture
majority of whom are small ranchers, fruit growers and farmers, because of the lack of co-operation between federal departments and between the dominion and provincial governments.

There is one subject I forgot to mention. I ask for the indulgence of the committee. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Monday we shall continue with the budget debate and if, as may be hoped for, we complete it, we shall spend the rest of the day on the budget resolutions. If they happen to be disposed of we shall go on with the Japanese trade treaty; but if Monday is taken up on the budget and the resolutions we shall take the Japanese trade treaty when we reach it on Tuesday and legislation which I can indicate on Monday evening to follow that.
